title: Why Can't You See Most of Hawaii? (Look Down)

segments.text: This is Hawaii's Big Island, with the ocean {m:drained}drained away.
segments.visual: S4 GROUND hero. FRAME 1 = THUMBNAIL ARM A (NO OCEAN, round-3 default, packaging/final_ep02_1.jpg) IN MOTION. TerrainStage with the plate d3 settings (landSat 1.6, landGain 2.7, darker cool basalt and sediment; masked grade: saturated rainforest green and rust on the cap, cool slate flank, deeper blue sky top), VE 1.0. Camera lon -155.32, lat 18.42, 26 km up, looking north; framing = the 1.32 zoom crop (centre 0.47/0.49); frame 0 must score SSIM >= 0.8 at 320x180 (label off) against final_ep02_1.jpg. No water anywhere in frame. The thin, solid, terrain-following white line on today's 0 m coast is on from frame 0 (never dashed, straight or labelled). Motion from frame 0: slow push 2%/10 s plus 0.3 deg/s heading drift. The thumbnail's 'NO OCEAN' text block is on frame 0 and dissolves out over 8 frames starting 0.6 s after {m:drained}. No gauge yet.
segments.music: Cold-open cue: airy, curious pulse from frame 1. No logo, no sting.

segments.text: {m:most}Most of this mountain is normally {m:under}underwater.
segments.visual: Same camera, push continues. At {m:most}: a 2.5 s eased tilt DOWN (pitch about -5 deg) along the south flank, from the white line toward the base (first hint of '(Look Down)'). At {m:under}: the white coast line brightens over 6 frames and back, so the eye finds where the sea normally stops. No text.

segments.text: The Hawaii on the {m:card}postcards? Only the {m:top}top.
segments.visual: At {m:card}: the sea snaps back: live refill from the base to 0 m in 1.2 s (water plane rises past the foreground flank, foam rim, turquoise depth gradient), leaving only the familiar island. In the same beat a paper postcard drops in from the top (off-white #F6F1E4, a real public-domain photo of a Big Island coast, place name 'HAWAIʻI' in large postcard type, tilted 4 deg, upper third, 35% of frame width, soft shadow). At {m:top}: a hero-orange outline (#FF5A36, 55% fill, 5-6 px white outline) traces only the dry cap above the water for 1.0 s.

segments.text: Let's drain it again, {m:step}step by step.
segments.visual: The postcard flutters off frame-right. At {m:step}: eased 2.0 s flight northwest (ease on the destination key) to Maui Nui at regional oblique, landing on the arm B 'ONE ISLAND' composition (packaging/final_ep02_2.jpg camera: south of Lānaʻi, about 60 km up, looking NNW), VE 1.0, water at 0 m. Persistent SEA LEVEL gauge top-left (plate 12-15% of frame height, moving water marker, no running digits) slides in during the flight.

segments.text: Drop the sea {m:400}four hundred {m:feet}feet.
segments.visual: HERO SHOT #1 (arm B composition). S4 GROUND live drain: water eases 0 to -122 m over 4 s. At {m:400}: the gauge goes to hero mode: a yellow #FFD23F Anton counter (cap 150-190 px) rolls to '−400 FT' and lands exactly on {m:feet}. Banks surface as cream-tan reef flats; Penguin Bank rises as a big flat lobe off West Molokaʻi.

segments.text: {m:maui}Maui, {m:molo}Molokai and {m:lanai}Lanai become one {m:one}island.
segments.visual: Same camera; water held at -122 m (never below -150 m in this shot, or Kahoʻolawe joins). One label at a time, pinned on its island (Barlow 800 caps, 64 px cap, plate with accent bar, 6-frame fades): MAUI at {m:maui}, MOLOKAʻI at {m:molo}, LĀNAʻI at {m:lanai}. At {m:one}: labels fade and the fused island (Molokaʻi + Lānaʻi + West Maui + Haleakalā + Penguin Bank; outline from sill.py flood-fill at -122 m on the production grid) takes the hero-orange 55% fill and white outline; headline 'ONE ISLAND' in the free third. The Pailolo Channel stays water (a bay inside the horseshoe). Kahoʻolawe stays separate, dimmed and desaturated, no label; Oʻahu and the Big Island stay separate.

segments.text: That's not a what-if. In the last {m:ice}Ice Age, they really were one island.
segments.visual: Low golden-hour pass (2.5 s, eased) over the dry land bridge between Lānaʻi and West Maui (the ʻAuʻau Channel floor near 20.885N 156.758W), camera 1.5 km up, VE 1.0, three seabirds crossing the dry channel at true scale. At {m:ice}: kicker 'LAST ICE AGE' in the top third for 2 s.

segments.text: No ferry {m:ferry}needed.
segments.visual: GAG (3.5 s), S11 paper standee on the real terrain. The recurring paper tourist (cut-out of a real public-domain 1950s Hawaiʻi tourist photo, aloha shirt; 2-4 px warm off-white paper edge, fold-out base tab, soft contact shadow, same sun) hop-walks across the dry ʻAuʻau Channel floor from Lānaʻi toward West Maui pulling a paper suitcase, at 35-40% of frame height, ground camera about 40 m up. The walk starts under the end of the previous line. At {m:ferry}: he tips his hat to camera. Never on the Pailolo side.
segments.humor: Deadpan: at the Ice Age low stand you could walk from Lānaʻi to Maui. 1.2 s music dip (-10 dB) right before the line; suitcase-wheel rattle in the gap after it.

segments.text: Keep draining. And {m:look}look down.
segments.visual: '(LOOK DOWN)' MOVE #1 (promise map: by about 0:27). At {m:look}: from the tourist the camera rises 300 m and pitches down 40 deg over Maui Nui's new north shore, then rides down the submarine slope as the water resumes falling (-122 m toward -1,000 m over 6 s; gauge marker dropping, no digits).

segments.text: The shore becomes a {m:ledge}ledge. Then the slope {m:plunge}plunges.
segments.visual: At {m:ledge}: the camera passes the edge of the shallow shelf; at {m:plunge}: it tips over and follows the submarine slope down (say 'plunges', never 'cliffs').

segments.text: See that flat {m:bank}bank? It was dry land once.
segments.visual: Eased 2 s pull-back and swing west: Penguin Bank, the big flat table off West Molokaʻi (top at about -30 to -60 m), stands high and dry above the falling water. At {m:bank}: hero-orange outline on the bank top; map label 'PENGUIN BANK'.

segments.text: It's the top of a {m:volc}volcano that sank, and coral grew over {m:over}it.
segments.visual: S4 cut-away ('cake cut') through the bank: a dark basalt volcano under a cream reef cap. At {m:volc}: the basalt core glows briefly and drops a little (sinking cue); at {m:over}: the reef cap highlights.

segments.text: Some of this land drowned when the sea rose after the Ice {m:age}Age.
segments.visual: The cut-away closes. At {m:age}: reverse drain, 3 s: the water rises from -1,000 m back to 0 m over Maui Nui; the land bridge and Penguin Bank go under and Maui, Molokaʻi and Lānaʻi separate again. Gauge marker climbs.

segments.text: The rest is slower. These islands {m:sink}sink as they age.
segments.visual: Pull back to a chain oblique (≤3 s). At {m:sink}: a short yellow down-arrow (15 px body) beside each main island pulses once, oldest (northwest) first.

segments.text: And the Big Island is sinking {m:now}right now, a little every year.
segments.visual: Whip-pan (8 frames, motion blur) southeast to the Big Island's south coast, sea at 0 m, morning light. At {m:now}: one yellow down-arrow beside the coast pulses once (no number).

segments.text: Usually, that's slow. {m:not}Not always.
segments.visual: Eased push toward Kīlauea's south-flank coast while the light falls to pre-dawn blue. Music thins out on {m:not}.
segments.music: Cold-open cue resolves and thins to a low sustained pad (no sting).

segments.text: In {m:yr}nineteen seventy-five, campers were sleeping at {m:hal}Halape, a beach on this coast.
segments.visual: RE-HOOK, human story. Close S4 GROUND shot on the USGS 3DEP 10 m DEM of the south coast at Halapē (pin from GNIS/NPS): a small cove, coconut palms at true scale, a few small tents among them (no people shown), still water, stars. At {m:yr}: kicker 'NOVEMBER 1975' (small, top-left of the free third, 2 s). At {m:hal}: map label 'HALAPĒ' on its pin.

segments.text: Before dawn, a smaller earthquake woke them {m:woke}up.
segments.visual: At {m:woke}: a short tremor: the palms shiver, the water surface ripples, a lantern glow comes on inside one tent.

segments.text: More than an hour later, the big one {m:hit}hit.
segments.visual: Hold on the quiet cove for 1.5 s, then at {m:hit}: a hard jolt (camera shake 6 frames), dust off the low cliff behind the grove.

segments.text: The south coast {m:lurch}lurched toward the sea.
segments.visual: At {m:lurch}: the whole coastal block slides seaward about 2 m in one move; quick pull-up to show a long stretch of coast moving together.

segments.text: The ground gave way. Parts of the shore {m:drop}dropped farther than a basketball hoop is high.
segments.visual: At {m:drop}: the coastal block subsides about 3.5 m in 1.5 s and the sea floods in among the palms. The palms STAY STANDING, now in about 1.2 m of water (visual truth). A true-scale paper basketball pole and hoop (rim at 10 ft) stands on the old shore beside the new edge; the drop visibly exceeds the rim. No numbers on screen.

segments.text: Within seconds, the sea rushed {m:rush}in.
segments.visual: At {m:rush}: a local wave surges over the dropped shore from the east (frame right) and fills the low ground; framed at human scale, never as a hero wave; the palms remain, a few low bushes are torn out.

segments.text: {m:two}Two people died.
segments.visual: Hold on the flooded grove at first light: wide, slow drift back, colour desaturated 20%. Optional [PD] USGS 'Submerged coconut grove at Halapē after 1975 quake' (marked Public Domain), full-bleed, Ken Burns 2%, 3 s max, starting just after {m:two}. No text, no gag, no sting.
segments.music: Single sustained low note; music down 3 dB.

segments.text: That was one side of one volcano, sliding a few {m:yards}yards.
segments.visual: Pull back to a regional oblique of the Big Island's south side; Kīlauea's south flank gets the hero-orange fill; at {m:yards}: a short yellow arrow points seaward.

segments.text: Now picture a whole side of a volcano letting {m:go}go.
segments.visual: At {m:go}: whip-pan northwest along the chain (8 frames, motion blur) toward Oʻahu. Chapter card 'OʻAHU'S MISSING SIDE' rides over the moving bright shot (near-opaque plate, 0.26 s in, 1.1 s hold, 0.26 s out); the voice gap covers the card's first 0.9 s.
segments.music: Crossfade to the Ch2 cue: lighter, windy, playful.

segments.text: This is the {m:pali}Pali Lookout, on {m:oahu}Oahu.
segments.visual: S3 HERO OBLIQUE settling into a ground shot: Nuʻuanu Pali State Wayside (pin from DLNR/GNIS), the green fluted Koʻolau cliffs, trade-wind clouds streaming over the ridge. Camera behind the railing at about 1,200 ft, looking northeast over the windward side. Map label 'PALI LOOKOUT' at {m:pali}; it fades at {m:oahu}.

segments.text: Pali means {m:cliff}cliff.
segments.visual: At {m:cliff}: the camera tilts to take in the full height of the cliff face below the railing.

segments.text: From the railing, the cliff drops away below your {m:feet}feet.
segments.visual: At {m:feet}: the camera leans over the railing and looks straight down the cliff face for 1.5 s, then pulls back to the railing.

segments.text: The wind here is usually so strong, you can {m:lean}lean on it.
segments.visual: The recurring paper tourist (same card as 0:25) stands at the railing at 35-40% of frame height. The trade wind blows FROM the northeast, up the cliff, into his face. At {m:lean}: he leans forward into the wind at an absurd 25-30 deg and stays up (paper hinge wobble, shirt flutter).

segments.text: Hold on to your {m:hat}hat.
segments.visual: GAG (3 s): at {m:hat} his hat lifts off and flies BACKWARD over his head, inland toward Honolulu (physically true for a wind blowing into his face); he turns and runs after it out of frame-left. The camera does NOT follow him: it tips over the railing and dives down the cliff face alone ('(Look Down)' echo, 2 s eased). Nothing and nobody falls off the Pali.
segments.humor: The joke is the wind, not the drop (taste: the 1795 battle). Gust plus a comic paper flap in the gap after the line.

segments.text: If you've stood here, you may have stood at the edge of a giant {m:break}break.
segments.visual: The dive levels out and pulls back to a regional oblique of windward Oʻahu from the northeast, 30 km up: the Koʻolau pali reads as one long curved wall. At {m:break}: a thin white line traces the cliff top.

segments.text: Rain has worn these cliffs back. But they may trace where a volcano tore {m:tore}apart.
segments.visual: At {m:tore}: a soft hero-orange glow runs along the cliff line (the scar). Nothing is drawn offshore.

segments.text: Hawaii's volcanoes don't just grow. Sometimes, whole sides of them {m:collapse}collapse.
segments.visual: At {m:collapse}: the camera starts to pull away from the cliffs out to sea (eased 2 s), the windward coast sliding below frame.

segments.text: To find the rest of that volcano, drain the sea {m:ne}northeast of Oahu.
segments.visual: At {m:ne}: eased 2.5 s move out to sea: camera about 80 km northeast of Oʻahu, 25 km up, looking southwest back at the island, VE 1.0, low sun from the east so the blocks will throw long shadows, hypsometric seabed tint (never grey mush). The live drain starts (water 0 to -4,500 m over the next 10 s, gauge marker dropping).

segments.text: Past the {m:shelf}shelf. Down the {m:slope}slope.
segments.visual: Same live drain: at {m:shelf} the shallow shelf around Oʻahu surfaces; at {m:slope} the water drops down the island's submarine slope.

segments.text: {m:first}First, the tops of giant blocks. Then {m:more}more blocks. Then a whole {m:field}field of rubble.
segments.visual: Same live drain, physically true order (highest points surface first): at {m:first} the tops of the tallest blocks break the falling water surface (the largest summit is at about -2,691 m); at {m:more} more blocks surface one after another (a new one every 1-2 s), spreading northeast; at {m:field} the lower, hummocky debris field emerges around them.

segments.text: This is the debris of one of the largest {m:slides}landslides on Earth.
segments.visual: At {m:slides}: the whole debris field (outline traced from USGS I-2809 / Moore et al. 1989, never invented) takes the hero-orange 55% fill and white outline.

segments.text: The volcano that built eastern Oahu split right through its {m:summit}summit.
segments.visual: Eased 2 s swing back toward Oʻahu's east side. At {m:summit}: a white line marks where the old summit caldera was cut in two (schematic marker on the real cliffs).

segments.text: Its whole northeast side is lying out {m:here}here.
segments.visual: At {m:here}: fast eased flight (2 s) from the cliffs out along the debris field; blocks rush past in the foreground.

segments.text: It broke away more than a million years {m:ago}ago. Then it slid out across the sea floor.
segments.visual: The camera follows the debris path outward along the real deposit at low altitude (the path is the mapped deposit, never a simulated collapse; no tsunami). At {m:ago}: no text (keep the screen clean); the deposit outline pulses once.

segments.text: Look at this one {m:block}block.
segments.visual: RE-HOOK. At {m:block}: push in to the largest block (summit about -2,691 m at 22.065N 157.072W; never name it), low sun, long shadow, VE 1.0, water now below its base.

segments.text: It's bigger than {m:manh}Manhattan.
segments.visual: HERO SHOT, S7 TRUE-SIZE DRAG: at {m:manh} a true-scale Manhattan outline (US Census TIGER New York County polygon, public domain; 5-6 px white outline, 40% cyan fill) drops from above and lands on the block's summit area at VE 1.0. Map label 'MANHATTAN' on the outline.

segments.text: With room to {m:spare}spare.
segments.visual: Dry gag (2.5 s): the outline slides around on the block, turns 20 deg and still has room on every side; at {m:spare} it settles into a corner with a tiny 'tok'.
segments.humor: A true-size drag that fits far too easily. Music dip before the line.

segments.text: And that's just one {m:just}block.
segments.visual: At {m:just}: the camera pulls up and away from the Manhattan block; dozens of other blocks come into frame around it.

segments.text: The debris runs for more than a hundred {m:miles}miles.
segments.visual: HERO NUMBER #2: pull back to a regional oblique; a 10 px yellow line with a moving head dot draws along the mapped deposit (USGS I-2809) from Oʻahu's coast out to the farthest blocks; at {m:miles} the number block lands: kicker 'MORE THAN', number '100 MILES'.

segments.text: And this isn't the only {m:one}one.
segments.visual: At {m:one}: the camera starts a quick pullback over the main islands.

segments.text: It's one of dozens of giant slides around these {m:isl}islands.
segments.visual: Same pullback (≤4 s): about 8-10 other giant slide footprints (traced only from USGS I-2809 / Moore et al. 1989) light up in hero orange, one every 0.25 s, finishing on {m:isl}.

segments.text: Their debris lies on the sea floor, out of {m:sight}sight.
segments.visual: At {m:sight}: the lit footprints sit on the drained sea floor; a quick ghost of today's water surface slides over them (0.5 s) to show they are normally hidden, then clears.

segments.text: They're rare. But they {m:happen}happen.
segments.visual: The footprints hold, then dim to 30% after {m:happen}.

segments.text: The coast that dropped in the dark? It's part of Kilauea's south {m:flank}flank.
segments.visual: Eased 2.5 s flight back southeast to the Big Island. At {m:flank}: Kīlauea's south flank outlined in hero orange; map label 'KĪLAUEA'.

segments.text: Big earthquakes there often come from that flank {m:slip}slipping toward the sea.
segments.visual: At {m:slip}: a short seaward nudge of the outlined flank (schematic, 0.5 s), with a faint rumble.

segments.text: And it's still {m:creep}creeping toward the sea.
segments.visual: At {m:creep}: small yellow arrows on the flank point seaward and inch forward (no rate, no digits).

segments.text: Not falling. {m:creeping}Creeping.
segments.visual: At {m:creeping}: the arrows keep inching; nothing collapses.

segments.text: Instruments on the flank record that motion {m:nonstop}nonstop.
segments.visual: At {m:nonstop}: small GPS-station icons (≥64 px) on the flank pulse once each.

segments.text: So how big is the mountain under the Big Island, {m:really}really?
segments.visual: At {m:really}: the camera rises to a high oblique of the whole Big Island, water at 0 m.

segments.text: Let's drain all the way {m:down}down.
segments.visual: At {m:down}: the drain starts (the water plane begins to fall). Chapter card 'THE ISLAND STANDS UP' over the moving drain shot.
segments.music: Crossfade to the Ch3 cue: big, rising, wide.

segments.text: Drain this far, and the islands stop being {m:isl}islands.
segments.visual: RE-HOOK. S4 GROUND live drain on the Big Island, low camera off the northeast flank (about 35 km northeast of Hilo, 1,000 m above the falling waterline, looking southwest), water -1,000 to -4,000 m over 8 s, gauge marker dropping. At {m:isl}: a quick high pullback (≤4 s) shows that by about -4,000 m every main island from the Big Island to Niʻihau sits on one continuous dry ridge (approximate ETOPO sill check; confirm on the HMRG grid before any label).

segments.text: It's one long mountain {m:range}range.
segments.visual: At {m:range}: a hero-orange line runs along the ridge crest from Hawaiʻi to Niʻihau, then fades.

segments.text: And at this end, the Big Island stands {m:up}up.
segments.visual: Eased 2 s dive back to the Big Island end of the ridge, low camera; at {m:up} the whole massif towers over the frame. Do NOT animate volcanoes merging: they are already one island; the drain only reveals the body.

segments.text: Several volcanoes grew together into this one {m:mtn}mountain.
segments.visual: At {m:mtn}: the summits of the island's volcanoes each get a brief white pin pulse (no names, no count), then the whole massif one hero-orange outline.

segments.text: Without the ocean, you can finally see its {m:shape}shape. Every ridge down here is {m:real}real.
segments.visual: At {m:shape}: slow lateral move along the base of the massif, low sun raking the real ridges and gullies of the submarine flanks (VE 1.0, HMRG 50 m synthesis blended into ETOPO). At {m:real}: the camera passes close over one ridge so its detail fills the foreground. Never put the 'real' line on screen.

segments.text: Today's shoreline is a thin white line, way up near the {m:top}top.
segments.visual: At {m:top}: the thin white coast line on the standing massif brightens; the camera holds it in the upper third of frame.

segments.text: Every beach you could ever visit is up {m:above}there.
segments.visual: At {m:above}: the cap above the white line (the dry island) takes a soft hero-orange tint for 1 s.

segments.text: Below it, the mountain keeps {m:going}going. And {m:going2}going.
segments.visual: '(Look Down)' beat inside the chapter: at {m:going} the camera tilts down the flank from the white line; at {m:going2} it keeps tilting, down and down to the base.

segments.text: Along its east side, the sea floor dips into a deep {m:trench}trench.
segments.visual: Water continues to about -5,500 m. The last water is the real strip in the Hawaiian Deep, from north of Molokaʻi and Maui to about 100 km east of Hilo (flood-fill at the shot's level on the real grid; west and south-west of the island are dry; NO sculpted ring). At {m:trench}: the leftover band glows bright cyan.

segments.text: It's the deepest water left around these {m:deep}islands.
segments.visual: At {m:deep}: the camera skims low along the cyan strip.

segments.text: Remember that {m:rem}trench.
segments.visual: At {m:rem}: slow push toward the cyan strip; one soft pulse. No label. (Loop planted; paid at the payoff.)

segments.text: Now bring in {m:ev}Everest, at the same scale.
segments.visual: S4 comparison shot, VE 1.0: at {m:ev} the SRTM Everest mesh rises (3 s, rumble) beside the massif, camera about 120 km to the north, 70 mm, low. Everest's summit stands 8,849 m above the shared base line (fill the gap under the SRTM mesh with a plain pedestal; never the 5,000 m base cut). Map label 'EVEREST'.

segments.text: Above sea level, Everest wins {m:easily}easily.
segments.visual: At {m:easily}: a thin white sea-level line across both; above it, Everest towers over Mauna Kea's cap.

segments.text: But measured from the sea floor, Mauna Kea is more than thirty-three thousand feet {m:tall}tall.
segments.visual: HERO NUMBER #3: a yellow height bar climbs Mauna Kea from the USGS base line (-6,000 m) to the summit while a counter rolls; it lands '33,000+ FT' exactly on {m:tall} (a label, never driven by the rendered moat floor). Kicker 'FROM THE SEA FLOOR'. Map label 'MAUNA KEA' on the summit.

segments.text: That's taller than {m:ev2}Everest.
segments.visual: At {m:ev2}: the bar's top passes Everest's summit on the same base line; a thin white tick marks Everest's top.

segments.text: You may have heard that {m:heard}one.
segments.visual: At {m:heard}: JUICE CHECK stamp 'TRUE' (S13, 1.2 s) over the still-moving comparison shot.

segments.text: On Everest, getting to the top looks like {m:this}this.
segments.visual: GAG part 1 (3 s), S11 on Everest's summit (SRTM terrain, real snow): at {m:this} a paper cut-out climber (public-domain photo, for example an NPS mountaineering photo; down suit, oxygen mask; not a named person) at 35-40% of frame height, frost on the card edge, plants a small flag while the card shudders in the wind.

segments.text: There's a road almost to the top of this {m:road}one.
segments.visual: GAG part 2: at {m:road} whip-pan (8 frames) to Mauna Kea's summit access road on the upper slope, well below the summit area: a paper 4WD (public-domain photo) rolls up the road with a little dust. Whip back: the climber's flag droops on its paper hinge. No car or figure on Puʻuwēkiu, no telescope joke; the domes are never the punchline.
segments.humor: The joke lands on the climber's ordeal. Music dip before the line; comic 'deflate' in the gap after it.

segments.text: But Mauna Kea isn't the giant {m:giant}here.
segments.visual: At {m:giant}: eased 2 s orbit to the southwest of the massif; Mauna Kea dims.

segments.text: Its neighbor, {m:loa}Mauna Loa, is a little lower, and far {m:bigger}bigger.
segments.visual: At {m:loa}: Mauna Loa's whole edifice, above and below the old waterline, takes the hero-orange fill and white outline; map label 'MAUNA LOA'. At {m:bigger}: the fill swells across its full broad mass beside the dimmed Mauna Kea.

segments.text: It's the largest {m:active}active volcano on Earth.
segments.visual: At {m:active}: headline 'LARGEST ACTIVE VOLCANO' (the qualifier 'ACTIVE' always stays) in the free third.

segments.text: It erupted again only a few years {m:ago}ago.
segments.visual: At {m:ago}: a faint warm glow traces a lava-flow path on Mauna Loa's flank (picture only, no date on screen).

segments.text: It covers more of this island than all the other volcanoes {m:comb}combined.
segments.visual: 3 s cut to today's island at sea level, high oblique: Mauna Loa's above-sea outline (USGS geologic map) fills in hero orange and the other volcanoes' areas in dim white; at {m:comb} the orange visibly outweighs the rest.

segments.text: And even now, we haven't seen all of {m:all}it.
segments.visual: Back to the drained massif; at {m:all} the camera lowers toward Mauna Loa's base, where the slope disappears into the trench shadow; slow push. (Loop: paid at the payoff.)

segments.text: Here's the twist. This giant is already {m:moving}moving.
segments.visual: TWIST. S4 cut-away under the Big Island: a glowing hot spot below (picture only, no labels). At {m:moving}: the plate carrying the island begins to slide northwest off the glow.

segments.text: It's riding away from the heat that {m:built}built it.
segments.visual: At {m:built}: the island's base slides past the edge of the glow.

segments.text: And as it goes, it {m:sinks}sinks.
segments.visual: At {m:sinks}: hard cut to the drained west (Kohala) flank at low raking light.

segments.text: See those {m:steps}steps on its side? They're old coral {m:reefs}reefs.
segments.visual: S4 GROUND close on the drowned-reef terraces off west Hawaiʻi (the documented series off Kohala; draw or highlight steps only where the bathymetry really shows terraces). At {m:steps}: the terrace edges catch the light; at {m:reefs}: a thin cream highlight runs along each step.

segments.text: They grew at the shoreline, and the island sank out from under {m:them}them.
segments.visual: Short schematic loop on one step (3 s): a reef grows at the waterline, then the step and the reef ride down as the water line stays; at {m:them} the next reef starts at the new shoreline above.

segments.text: The deepest ones are now thousands of feet {m:deepreef}down.
segments.visual: At {m:deepreef}: the camera tilts down the flank along the lowest terraces into the dark (no depth text).

segments.text: Every island to the northwest was born right here, over the same hot {m:spot}spot.
segments.visual: At {m:spot}: regional pullback (≤4 s) along the chain to the northwest; each main island takes a brief hero-orange rim in turn (Maui, Oʻahu, Kauaʻi).

segments.text: Each one is older than the {m:last}last.
segments.visual: At {m:last}: the rims fade in order of age, youngest to oldest.

segments.text: And each one shows what this island will {m:become}become.
segments.visual: At {m:become}: the camera settles back on the Big Island. Chapter card 'WATCH IT GROW OLD' over the moving shot.
segments.music: Crossfade to the Ch4 cue: travelling, steady pulse.

segments.text: Here's how it works. Picture a {m:candle}candle under a sheet of paper.
segments.visual: Physical metaphor in motion (the whole metaphor ≤20 s, no jargon on screen): at {m:candle}, in the cut-away under the Big Island, the plate becomes a sheet of paper with a candle flame beneath it (the flame sits where the hot-spot glow was).

segments.text: Slide the paper slowly, and the flame scorches a line of {m:spots}spots.
segments.visual: The paper slides; a line of scorch marks forms; at {m:spots} the marks cross-dissolve (0.5 s) into the real island chain at chain oblique.

segments.text: Here, the paper is the Pacific {m:plate}plate, sliding {m:nw}northwest.
segments.visual: Back on the real Earth: at {m:plate} the Pacific plate takes a 35% hero-orange tint; at {m:nw}: a big yellow arrow (15 px body, 50-63 px head) points northwest along the chain.

segments.text: The flame is a hot spot, deep {m:below}below.
segments.visual: At {m:below}: the cut-away glow under the Big Island returns for 1.5 s (picture only, no 'plume from the core' label).

segments.text: That makes the Big Island the baby of the {m:chain}chain.
segments.visual: At {m:chain}: the Big Island alone takes a hero-orange rim at the young end of the lit chain.

segments.text: And age treats every island here the same {m:here}way.
segments.visual: At {m:here}: chain oblique; each step lights as it is named in the next line.

segments.text: The volcano goes {m:quiet}quiet. Rain wears it {m:wear}down. And it {m:sinks}sinks.
segments.visual: Three quick schematic beats on one generic island cross-section (no labels): at {m:quiet} the summit glow goes out; at {m:wear} valleys cut into the slope; at {m:sinks} the whole island lowers against a fixed waterline.

segments.text: So let's ride the plate, and watch the Big Island grow {m:old}old.
segments.visual: RE-HOOK, THE TIME MACHINE (the film's second engine). For this chapter the top-left gauge becomes an AGE gauge (same corner and plate; a yellow marker on a slim bar, starting at 'NOW'). At {m:old}: eased flight northwest begins; each island fills at least a third of the frame at regional oblique; real islands at their real positions, no morphing.

segments.text: Give it time, and it looks like {m:maui}Maui.
segments.visual: Flight lands on Maui (Haleakalā fills the frame). At {m:maui}: map label 'MAUI'; the age marker slides right.

segments.text: Its big volcano, {m:hale}Haleakala, last erupted only a few centuries ago.
segments.visual: At {m:hale}: map label 'HALEAKALĀ' on the summit; a faint dark young-lava tone on its lower flank (picture only).

segments.text: At its biggest, Maui's joined island was bigger than today's Big {m:big}Island.
segments.visual: S7 TRUE-SIZE DRAG: at {m:big} a white outline of today's Big Island (true size) slides over to sit beside Maui Nui; draw Maui Nui's 'at its biggest' outline ONLY if a published reconstruction (Price & Elliott-Fisk 2004 / USGS 2003) can be traced; otherwise compare against the -400 ft island and narrate without the outline.

segments.text: Now look at {m:it}it.
segments.visual: At {m:it}: the outline fades; today's three separate islands, sea at 0 m.

segments.text: Older still: {m:oahu}Oahu, where a whole side of a volcano slid into the sea.
segments.visual: Flight to Oʻahu's windward side, the Koʻolau cliffs and the debris field offshore. At {m:oahu}: map label 'OʻAHU'. Callback GAG (2 s): back at the Pali Lookout, the paper tourist now holds his hat on with both hands.

segments.text: Older still: {m:kauai}Kauai, carved into {m:canyons}canyons.
segments.visual: Flight to Kauaʻi. At {m:kauai}: map label 'KAUAʻI'; at {m:canyons}: the camera drops into the red walls of Waimea Canyon.

segments.text: Its volcanoes went quiet long ago. Since then, rain has been {m:rain}carving it.
segments.visual: At {m:rain}: a rain squall sweeps over the canyon rim; water threads down the gullies.

segments.text: After that, the islands get smaller and {m:lower}lower.
segments.visual: At {m:lower}: fast eased flight northwest past Niʻihau and out over open ocean; the age marker keeps sliding right.

segments.text: This is {m:nihoa}Nihoa.
segments.visual: RE-HOOK. Nihoa fills the frame: a small steep island with tall sea cliffs. At {m:nihoa}: map label 'NIHOA'.

segments.text: {m:seven}Seven million years in, it's a sliver of {m:rock}rock.
segments.visual: HERO NUMBER #4: at {m:seven} the AGE gauge marker lands and the number block lands: kicker 'ABOUT', number '7 MILLION YEARS' (Anton, yellow); at {m:rock} the camera pulls wide to show how little is left; the block fades before the next line.

segments.text: And people {m:lived}lived here.
segments.visual: At {m:lived}: slow push into Nihoa's terraced valleys; music softens.

segments.text: Centuries ago, they built homes, farm terraces and shrines on this {m:shrine}rock.
segments.visual: [PD] USFWS or NOAA Nihoa photo (credit line checked), full-bleed, Ken Burns 2%, 3 s max, landing on {m:shrine}; then back on our terrain, where house and terrace sites appear only as drawn from a published site map (otherwise marked approximate or left out). No gags here (there are burials).

segments.text: Archaeologists have found dozens of sites here, even {m:graves}graves.
segments.visual: At {m:graves}: small white markers (≥64 px) fade in on the real site positions from a published site map only (otherwise none); slow drift, no gag.

segments.text: Some probably lived here all year {m:year}round.
segments.visual: At {m:year}: slow drift over the terraces in late light.

segments.text: Today, nobody {m:nobody}does.
segments.visual: At {m:nobody}: wind over empty rock; seabird specks; pull away.

segments.text: It's a protected refuge now, part of a marine {m:monument}monument.
segments.visual: At {m:monument}: map label 'PAPAHĀNAUMOKUĀKEA' fades in over the northwest chain for 2.5 s (label only; the name is not narrated).

segments.text: Farther on: French Frigate {m:ffs}Shoals. In Hawaiian, {m:lalo}Lalo.
segments.visual: Eased flight northwest to the lagoon at Lalo. At {m:ffs}: map label 'LALO (FRENCH FRIGATE SHOALS)' fades in and holds through {m:lalo}.

segments.text: One rock is all that's left of its volcano. La Perouse Pinnacle, its last {m:tooth}tooth.
segments.visual: Close oblique on the lone basalt pinnacle standing out of the lagoon; at {m:tooth}: hero-orange outline on the pinnacle; map label 'LA PÉROUSE PINNACLE'. No height spoken or shown.

segments.text: It's named after a French explorer who nearly {m:wreck}wrecked here.
segments.visual: At {m:wreck}: a small paper sailing-ship cut-out (public-domain engraving) bobs past the pinnacle and swerves away from the reef (2 s, light).

segments.text: Not long ago, a hurricane passed right over these {m:shoals}shoals.
segments.visual: At {m:shoals}: a storm spiral (soft cloud texture, true colour, no category label) sweeps over the lagoon from the southeast (2 s).

segments.text: It washed almost all of East Island {m:away}away.
segments.visual: Before/after on our terrain from dated imagery (July 2018 vs October 2018): East Island's sandy outline (map label 'EAST ISLAND'), then at {m:away} a wipe shrinks it to a sliver. No storm category, no 'overnight'.

segments.text: Hawaiian monk seals are endangered, and these shoals are one of their key {m:nursery}nurseries.
segments.visual: At {m:nursery}: before-state on the old East Island sand: a paper monk seal (public-domain NOAA photo; grey-brown, no ear flaps) resting at 35-40% of frame height.

segments.text: They used this island to rest and raise {m:pups}pups.
segments.visual: Before-state holds (the seal and a pup shape on the old sand). Then GAG (3 s) in the pause after {m:pups}: wipe to the after-state; the seal swims up to where the island was, finds water, bobs, looks left, looks right (paper turn), blinks. Nothing implies a seal was hurt.
segments.humor: The seal comes home and the beach is missing. Music dip; tiny comic 'bloop' in the gap.

segments.text: Since then, the sand has been coming {m:back}back.
segments.visual: At {m:back}: time-lapse from the monthly shorelines: the sand outline regrows to about half its old size (no percent on screen); keep it bare (no vegetation).

segments.text: And so have the {m:seals}seals.
segments.visual: At {m:seals}: the seal flops onto the regrown sandbar and settles; two more seals haul out beside it (real terrain, contact shadows, same sun).
segments.humor: Twist on the gag: the seals came back.

segments.text: Farther on, one last pair of rocks pokes {m:out}out.
segments.visual: Flight northwest: at {m:out} the Gardner Pinnacles appear, two small basalt rocks in open sea; map label 'PŪHĀHONU (GARDNER PINNACLES)'.

segments.text: After that, no volcanic rock reaches the surface at {m:all}all.
segments.visual: At {m:all}: the flight continues northwest over open water; the AGE marker slides on; pale reef rings appear ahead.

segments.text: Only {m:reef}reef.
segments.visual: At {m:reef}: arrival over a ring of reef. Chapter card 'FOUGHT OVER A VOLCANO' over the moving shot.
segments.music: Crossfade to the Ch5 cue: bright, open, a little mischievous.

segments.text: This ring of reef is {m:midway}Midway.
segments.visual: S3 HERO OBLIQUE: Midway Atoll (28.21N 177.37W), true colour, the reef ring and Sand Island at regional oblique. At {m:midway}: map label 'MIDWAY'. The top-left gauge is the SEA LEVEL gauge again.

segments.text: It sits far out in the Pacific, a long way northwest of {m:hnl}Honolulu.
segments.visual: At {m:hnl}: brief high pullback (≤3 s) with a thin line from Honolulu to Midway (no distance label); then back down to the atoll.

segments.text: It has the biggest albatross colony on {m:earth}Earth.
segments.visual: At {m:earth}: dive to Sand Island at ground level: a field of nesting albatrosses as small shapes; one paper Laysan albatross (public-domain USFWS photo) in the foreground at 35-40% of frame height.

segments.text: Most of the world's Laysan albatrosses nest {m:nest}here.
segments.visual: At {m:nest}: the camera skims low over the nesting field; map label 'LAYSAN ALBATROSS' for 2 s.

segments.text: In the air, they're {m:grace}graceful.
segments.visual: At {m:grace}: the paper albatross glides across the frame, wings out, smooth.

segments.text: Landing is another {m:story}story.
segments.visual: GAG (3 s): at {m:story} the albatross comes in to land in a light wind, wings out, and tumbles into a forward roll on the sand (believable, on the real terrain); dust puff; it ends upright and ruffled.
segments.humor: The clumsy landing. Music dip before the line; comic thump in the gap.

segments.text: Here, they're known as gooney {m:gooney}birds.
segments.visual: At {m:gooney}: the bird shakes its head; slow pull back up to the atoll.

segments.text: Under this reef lies a volcano about twenty-eight million years {m:old}old.
segments.visual: RE-HOOK, HERO NUMBER #5. Drain plus cut-away (S4 'cake cut'): the water falls around the atoll, then the atoll is sliced open: a dark basalt volcano under a thick cream reef cap. At {m:old}: number block 'ABOUT 28 MILLION YEARS' with a thin pointer to the basalt (the age belongs to the volcano, not the reef).

segments.text: As it sank, the reef on top kept growing {m:up}upward.
segments.visual: At {m:up}: the cut-away animates: the volcano sinks in uneven steps (pauses between them, never smooth) and the reef cap grows upward to stay at the surface.

segments.text: Charles {m:darwin}Darwin came up with this idea: reefs like this sit on sinking islands.
segments.visual: [PD] Darwin's 1842 coral-reef woodcut diagram (public domain) brought to life: its island layer sinks and its reef layer climbs (3 s, Ken Burns), never a portrait. Name plate 'CHARLES DARWIN' at {m:darwin}.

segments.text: He said he worked it out before he'd ever seen a true coral {m:reef}reef.
segments.visual: At {m:reef}: the woodcut's reef layer highlights.

segments.text: And he never came {m:here}here.
segments.visual: At {m:here}: back to the atoll cut-away.

segments.text: Long after he died, drills here went down through hundreds of feet of reef {m:rock}rock.
segments.visual: Cut-away: two drill strings (Sand Island, and the north rim of the lagoon) descend through the cream reef rock, reaching the bottom of it on {m:rock}; the basalt top sits about 515 ft under Sand Island and deepens to about 1,250 ft under the north rim (optional thin clay band on the basalt). No depth numbers on screen.

segments.text: And hit the {m:hit}volcano.
segments.visual: At {m:hit}: the bits strike basalt; a spark flash on the basalt top.

segments.text: In June {m:1942}nineteen forty-two, a battle was fought over this sunken {m:volc}volcano.
segments.visual: TWIST, RE-HOOK. Hard cut back to the atoll from above, water restored, early-morning light. At {m:1942}: kicker 'JUNE 1942'. At {m:volc}: the reef ring takes a thin hero-orange rim.
segments.music: Ch5 cue switches section to a taut pulse (story turn).

segments.text: It turned the war in the {m:pac}Pacific.
segments.visual: At {m:pac}: pull out to a regional S2 STORY map of the central Pacific centred on Midway.

segments.text: And part of the story is a fake complaint about {m:water0}water.
segments.visual: At {m:water0}: a paper water drop icon pops on Midway's pin and wobbles (story humour; no one has died yet).

segments.text: Weeks before, American codebreakers kept seeing one target in Japan's coded {m:msgs}messages: {m:af}AF.
segments.visual: At {m:msgs}: coded radio traffic drawn as scrambled glyph streams crossing the map; at {m:af}: the letters 'AF' light up yellow inside the stream.

segments.text: They were fairly sure AF was Midway. Washington {m:proof}wasn't.
segments.visual: At {m:proof}: a small paper telegram flutters from the Hawaiʻi side of the map toward the edge of frame (toward Washington), then flutters back with a paper question-mark tag (no readable text).

segments.text: So, by undersea cable, they quietly told Midway to send a message in plain {m:plain}language.
segments.visual: A thin glowing line runs along the sea floor on the map from Hawaiʻi to Midway (the secure cable; schematic, labelled nothing); at {m:plain}: a clean, readable radio ring pulses out from Midway into the air.

segments.text: Our fresh-water plant has broken {m:down}down.
segments.visual: At {m:down}: in-world, a paper water tank on Sand Island gives a sad little wobble and a drip. No quote marks and no message text on screen.

segments.text: Then a coded Japanese report passed it {m:along}along.
segments.visual: A scrambled glyph stream travels back across the map; at {m:along} it starts to decode.

segments.text: AF is short of {m:water}water.
segments.visual: At {m:water}: the stream resolves (no text block, just the glyph stream settling); music dip -10 dB under the line.
segments.humor: The punchline is the enemy repeating the fake plea.

segments.text: That {m:conf}confirmed it. AF was {m:mid2}Midway.
segments.visual: At {m:conf}: the question-mark tag falls off the telegram; at {m:mid2}: 'AF = MIDWAY' lands beside Midway's pin with a soft thunk (not the Juice Check stamp).

segments.text: Most of the fighting happened far out at {m:sea}sea.
segments.visual: At {m:sea}: the story map pulls out to open ocean north and west of Midway; music down a notch. No gags from here through the wreck beat.
segments.music: Pulse drops to a low, respectful pad.

segments.text: Japan lost every carrier in its strike {m:force}force.
segments.visual: At {m:force}: four simple home-built Japanese carrier silhouettes on the map fade down to dark grey one after another (no flames, no explosions).

segments.text: America lost the carrier {m:york}Yorktown.
segments.visual: At {m:york}: [PD] NHHC photo of USS Yorktown (check the catalog credit line), full-bleed, Ken Burns 2%, 3 s max.

segments.text: Badly damaged, it was finished off by a Japanese {m:sub}submarine.
segments.visual: At {m:sub}: back on the map, the Yorktown silhouette fades down to dark grey (no explosion, no torpedo animation).

segments.text: {m:york2}Yorktown, {m:kaga}Kaga and {m:akagi}Akagi have since been found.
segments.visual: Back on the map: one respectful wreck marker (home-built hull silhouette, ≥64 px) per name, each at its RECORDED 1942 sinking position (Yorktown 30°35'59"N 176°34'04"W; Akagi 30°30'N 178°40'W; Kaga 30°23'N 179°17'W; approximate at chain scale), with a map label on its word: YORKTOWN at {m:york2}, KAGA at {m:kaga}, AKAGI at {m:akagi}.

segments.text: Drain the sea, and you'd find them nowhere near the {m:atoll}atoll.
segments.visual: Drain the ocean around Midway on the GEBCO chain terrain; at {m:atoll} a thick yellow line (10 px core, dark under-stroke) draws from the atoll to each wreck marker; its length shows the distance (no distance labels, no coordinates).

segments.text: They lie far out, more than three miles {m:down}down, on the deep ocean floor.
segments.visual: Inset zoom (the wrecks are tiny at chain scale): low camera on the deep ocean floor (gentle abyssal hills, not flat), one hull silhouette resting in dim blue light; at {m:down} the SEA LEVEL gauge marker sits far down (no digits).

segments.text: A research ship has filmed each of {m:visit}them.
segments.visual: At {m:visit}: a small home-built ROV light glides past the resting silhouette (no real expedition imagery).

segments.text: These are war graves, for American and Japanese sailors {m:alike}alike.
segments.visual: At {m:alike}: hold, slow drift; music down to a soft pad. No gags, no 'treasure', no gore.
segments.music: Soft pad, then lift into the Kure section after the pause.

segments.text: Past Midway lies {m:kure}Kure, the last atoll in the chain.
segments.visual: Eased flight northwest to Kure Atoll (28.39N 178.29W), water restored, reef ring. At {m:kure}: map label 'KURE (HŌLANIKŪ)' (label only, not narrated).

segments.text: Darwin never saw it. But on his reef map, he colored it {m:blue}blue.
segments.visual: [PD] crop of Darwin's 1842 reef map (5 words or fewer visible), Ken Burns 3 s; at {m:blue}: Kure's spot on the old map glows blue.

segments.text: Blue meant a reef on sinking {m:ground}ground.
segments.visual: At {m:ground}: back to the real Kure; the reef ring tinted soft blue for 1 s.

segments.text: Here the water is so cool, the reef can barely keep up with the {m:sink}sinking.
segments.visual: Cut-away under Kure: the reef cap just keeping pace at the surface while the volcano sinks; at {m:sink} the reef's top flickers at the waterline.

segments.text: Scientists call this line the Darwin {m:point}Point.
segments.visual: At {m:point}: a thin hero-orange line across the chain at about 29N lights up; map label 'DARWIN POINT'.

segments.text: Past it, every island has {m:drowned}drowned.
segments.visual: At {m:drowned}: the water drains northwest of Kure (GEBCO): drowned flat-topped seamounts appear beyond the line.

segments.text: The drowned volcanoes {m:bend}bend north and march on, all the way to {m:kam}Kamchatka.
segments.visual: S2 STORY globe filling the frame height (≤4 s): the Hawaiian-Emperor chain lit in hero orange; at {m:bend} the bend lights up; at {m:kam} the line reaches Kamchatka; map label 'KAMCHATKA'. No bend age, no cause for the bend.

segments.text: There, the sea floor dives back into the Earth, and takes them with {m:it}it.
segments.visual: Close globe cut-away at the far end: at {m:it} the plate slides down under Kamchatka, carrying the last seamount down with it (no text, or at most 'TRENCH').

segments.text: That's where the Big Island is {m:headed}headed.
segments.visual: At {m:headed}: whip back down the chain to the Big Island (≤3 s).

segments.text: But every story on this conveyor starts {m:some}somewhere.
segments.visual: At {m:some}: chapter card 'WE HAVEN'T HIT BOTTOM' over the moving shot.
segments.music: Crossfade to the Ch6 cue: deep, building toward the payoff.

segments.text: Back to the start of the line: the Big Island's south {m:coast}coast.
segments.visual: RE-HOOK. At {m:coast}: fast eased flight southeast (2.5 s) down to the Big Island's south flank; water drained to about -1,500 m so the young volcano's top (-975 m) stands exposed; SEA LEVEL gauge back top-left.

segments.text: Just offshore, about thirty-two hundred feet {m:down}down, a young volcano is growing.
segments.visual: HERO NUMBER #6: the gauge marker drops to its summit level and the number block lands on {m:down}: '3,200 FT DOWN'. The volcano is rendered from the real bathymetry as an ELONGATED RIDGE with a summit platform and pit craters (never a neat cone), about 30 km south of Kīlauea's coast (18°55'12"N 155°16'12"W).

segments.text: Its name is {m:kama}Kamaehuakanaloa.
segments.visual: Map label 'KAMAʻEHUAKANALOA' fades in 4 frames before {m:kama} and stays at least 2.5 s. Own take, speed 0.9, about 0.4 s of silence before it, no other new proper noun within 10 s.

segments.text: It's thought to have erupted within living {m:mem}memory.
segments.visual: At {m:mem}: slow orbit along the ridge; a faint warm glow in one pit crater (picture only, no eruption shown).

segments.text: And this summer, it set off an earthquake people felt across the island's {m:south}south.
segments.visual: At {m:south}: soft felt-shaking rings spread from the volcano across the south of the island (no magnitude, no 'strong').

segments.text: You may know it by its old name, {m:loihi}Loihi.
segments.visual: At {m:loihi}: map label 'LŌʻIHI' for 2 s, below the main label's old position (the new name came first).

segments.text: It could become the next Hawaiian {m:next}island.
segments.visual: At {m:next}: slow push toward the summit platform.

segments.text: Opening date: thousands of years from now, at {m:least}least.
segments.visual: GAG (3 s): at {m:least} a paper 'COMING SOON' sign pops up on the summit platform on its paper hinge (close shot, sign at 35-40% of frame height), wobbles and settles.
segments.humor: The joke is the sign, never the name Kanaloa. Comic 'pop' in the gap.

segments.text: One day, people may watch it rise out of the {m:rise}sea.
segments.visual: At {m:rise}: a slow push up the volcano's flank toward the old sea-level line far above (ghost line, no water).

segments.text: So at one end of this chain, volcanoes are being {m:born}born.
segments.visual: At {m:born}: quick high pullback (≤3 s) along the whole chain: the young end glows warm.

segments.text: At the other, they're being {m:swallowed}swallowed.
segments.visual: At {m:swallowed}: the far (Kamchatka) end of the chain dims, then the camera dives back to the Big Island.

segments.text: Up on the coast, the waves are busy {m:too}too.
segments.visual: At {m:too}: eased rise up the flank to today's south coast near the end of Chain of Craters Road, water back at 0 m.

segments.text: This September, the sea arch at {m:holei}Holei collapsed into the ocean.
segments.visual: Before/after: the arch on our 10 m DEM coast (pinned from the NPS place page) or a public-domain NPS photo of the arch (credit line checked, 3 s max); at {m:holei} the arch is there, then a wipe to the gap where it stood. Map label 'HŌLEI SEA ARCH'. No cause shown or implied.

segments.text: Visitors drove to the end of a park road to see {m:see2}it.
segments.visual: At {m:see2}: the end of the park road above the coast, empty, with the gap in the sea cliff beyond.

segments.text: Nobody knows exactly when it {m:fall}fell.
segments.visual: At {m:fall}: waves wash through the gap.

segments.text: The waves had carved it out of lava over {m:cent}centuries.
segments.visual: At {m:cent}: slow pull back from the coast.

segments.text: We've drained the whole {m:whole}ocean.
segments.visual: RE-HOOK. At {m:whole}: drain again, all the way: pull out to the full Big Island massif with every bit of water gone from the frame except the cyan strip in the trench; gauge marker at the bottom of its bar.

segments.text: But we still haven't reached the bottom of this {m:bottom}mountain.
segments.visual: At {m:bottom}: slow push down toward the base.

segments.text: Remember that deep trench at its {m:feet}feet?
segments.visual: At {m:feet}: callback to the Ch3 plant: the cyan strip pulses once.

segments.text: Slice through the {m:rock}rock, and you'll see why it's there.
segments.visual: PAYOFF CUT-AWAY: at {m:rock} the terrain slices cleanly along a north-south plane through Mauna Loa; the crust and Moho sag beneath the island (schematic curve from the USGS flexure description, up to 8 km under Mauna Loa), with the trench at the edge of the sag.

segments.text: This island is so heavy, it has bent the sea floor {m:down}down.
segments.visual: At {m:down}: the sag deepens to its full shape in 1.5 s.

segments.text: Like a bowling ball on a {m:matt}mattress.
segments.visual: At {m:matt}: ≤3 s metaphor inset: a bowling ball sinks into a mattress; dissolve straight back to the cut-away.

segments.text: Under Mauna Loa, it's pushed down by {m:miles}miles.
segments.visual: At {m:miles}: a yellow line marks the dented true base under Mauna Loa.

segments.text: So this mountain doesn't sit on the sea floor. It sits in a {m:dent}dent.
segments.visual: At {m:dent}: the dented base line glows; the old flat sea-floor level is drawn as a faint white line across the sag for comparison.

segments.text: Look {m:look}down. Past the old sea floor, to the true {m:base}base.
segments.visual: '(LOOK DOWN)' MOVE #2: at {m:look} the camera tips down Mauna Loa's flank, past the trench and the old sea floor, through the cut, and arrives at the dented base line on {m:base}.

segments.text: Measured from its true base, Mauna Loa is about fifty-six thousand feet {m:tall}tall.
segments.visual: HERO NUMBER #7, THE PAYOFF: a yellow height bar climbs from the true base (about -13,000 m under the summit, from the USGS figures, not the DEM) to the summit while the counter rolls; it lands 'ABOUT 56,000 FT' on {m:tall}, kicker 'FROM ITS TRUE BASE'. The old sea-level line, the dented base line and the summit are in one frame, VE 1.0.
segments.music: Payoff swell; 1.2 s dip right before {m:tall}, full after.

segments.text: Almost twice as tall as {m:ev}Everest.
segments.visual: At {m:ev}: Everest (true scale, 8,849 m above the shared base line, VE 1.0) rises on the same dented base line beside Mauna Loa and reaches about halfway.

segments.text: Stand Everest on that same base, and its peak would still be deep {m:under}underwater.
segments.visual: At {m:under}: the old sea-level line glows white; Everest's summit sits far below it.

segments.text: That's how much of this mountain you never get to {m:see}see.
segments.visual: At {m:see}: the camera eases back to frame the whole cut-away, from the dented base to the summit, with the old sea-level line high up near the top.

segments.text: Now put the ocean {m:back}back.
segments.visual: THE REFILL, part A (live, ≤10 s per composition, level and camera moving): at {m:back} the cut-away closes and the water starts to rise from the dented base; the camera begins its continuous journey back toward the frame-1 composition (lon -155.32, lat 18.42, 26 km up, looking north, 1.32 crop).
segments.music: Opening theme returns under the refill.

segments.text: The trench fills {m:trench2}first. Then the {m:slopes}slopes.
segments.visual: THE REFILL, part B (new composition, camera still travelling): at {m:trench2} the cyan strip in the trench floods and spreads; at {m:slopes} the water climbs the lower flanks.

segments.text: Wave by wave, the postcard comes {m:pc}back.
segments.visual: At {m:pc}: the water climbs past the reef steps toward the white line; the familiar green-and-black island re-forms.

segments.text: And the giant {m:gone}disappears again.
segments.visual: At {m:gone}: the water reaches 0 m; only the familiar island is left.

segments.text: Every postcard of the Big Island shows only the top of a {m:giant}giant.
segments.visual: Frame-1 composition with the sea at 0 m; at {m:giant} the paper postcard from the cold open drops into the same spot.

segments.text: And that giant is slowly sinking, into the dent it pressed into the {m:planet}planet.
segments.visual: Hold the frame-1 composition, slow push; at {m:planet} a ghost of the dent shows under the island for 1.5 s, then fades. No end-screen element yet.

segments.text: And what happens when a whole lake drains down a {m:hole}hole?
segments.visual: HAND-OFF (within 0-3 s of the final line): at {m:hole} the postcard flips over to a Louisiana postcard of Lake Peigneur; the shot keeps moving.

segments.text: It happened in {m:la}Louisiana.
segments.visual: End-screen elements (the Lake Peigneur video large, plus Subscribe) appear only after {m:la} finishes (the last voiced word), over the still-moving refill shot (slow orbit, waves moving). Cut about 1 s after the word; the end screen runs about 11 s.
